comments.text: There is no such thing as Somaliland. Many Somalis call it Isaaqland, viewing it as a tribal claim over territory where the Isaaq clan resides, rather than representing the entire region shown on your map. replies.author: @MohamedAliNotTheBoxer
replies.text:
There is such a thing as Somaliland. It declared independence in 1991 as the successor to the brief independent State of Somaliland British Somaliland, 26 June–1 July 1960. It has its own government, parliament, currency, army, passports, and regular elections with peaceful power transfers and has been far more stable than the rest of Somalia for 35 years.
Calling it just “Isaaqland” is a deliberate oversimplification. Isaaq are the majority (roughly 70-80% in the core areas), but the claim is based on the colonial borders of British Somaliland, not pure tribalism. Other clans also live and participate within those borders.
The “only a quarter of the territory” claim is exaggerated. The demographic and economic heartland (Hargeisa, Berbera, Burao etc.) is firmly under Hargeisa’s control. The eastern Sool/Sanaag/Cayn areas are contested SSC-Khaatumo (mainly Dhulbahante) has aligned with Mogadishu and controls parts of that zone after 2023 fighting. That doesn’t erase the rest of Somaliland.
As of Dec 2025, Israel formally recognised it as a sovereign state. Most of the world still doesn’t, but a functioning de facto state with institutions, borders it controls, and now one formal recognition is not “non-existent.”

Almost correct. The following can be found in the African Unions fact finding mission to Somaliland in 2005:

Somaliland (the North) was a British Protectorate that gained independence on June 26th 1960, 5 days before the South (Somalia). This made it the first independent East African nation! But, due to the British ceding territory from Somaliland to Ethiopia, Somaliland fatally joined w Somalia on June 1st 1960 once the South gained independence. 

The union was never ratified and the South treated  Somaliland as a colony from 1960-1991. After rebellion mounted in the 1980s in Somaliland, the Somalia dominated government launched a war of erasure against the Isaaq which their own internal reports called “a final solution to the Isaaq problem.”

Despite this, Somaliland managed to remove the Somalia military from the borders of the OG Protectorate and re-established the brief entity that existed from June 26-July 1st 1969.

This wasn’t done out of love for the ol’ British entity, but because it followed the African standard of maintaining borders received at Independence.

Fun fact: Senegal and Gambia unified and dissolved their union during this period. Same thing with Egypt and Syria. Somaliland however hasn’t been allowed to disintegrate their failed union with Somalia for some reason despite the completely opposite security situation and political system :(
